lx-cli.heading: Finding files and getting help
body: Two commands answer most 'where is it?' questions. `find /var/log -name '*.log' -mtime -1` searches a directory tree by name, type, size or modification time and can act on what it finds (`-exec`, or `-delete` with care). `locate` searches a prebuilt index and is much faster, but only knows about files that existed at the last `updatedb` run. `which python3` shows which executable your shell will actually run.

When you meet an unfamiliar command, the documentation is already on the system. `man ls` opens the manual page, `ls --help` prints a short summary, and `apropos compress` searches manual page descriptions for a keyword. Tab completion saves typing and catches typos: press Tab once to complete a path, twice to list the options. `history` and Ctrl+R let you find and rerun earlier commands instead of retyping them.

lx-perms.heading: Access control lists and troubleshooting
body: The nine permission bits allow one owner, one group and everyone else. When you need more, for example giving a second team read access without changing the group, POSIX ACLs add entries per user or group: `setfacl -m u:ana:r report.txt` grants Ana read access, and `getfacl report.txt` shows the full list. A `+` at the end of the mode in `ls -l` output tells you a file has an ACL.

When access is denied, check every directory in the path, not just the file: a user needs execute (x) permission on each parent directory to reach a file inside it. `namei -l /srv/app/config.yml` lists the owner and mode of every component in one go. Also remember that SELinux or AppArmor can deny access even when the permission bits allow it; `ls -Z` shows SELinux labels and the audit log records the denials.

lx-users.heading: Managing accounts safely
body: Day-to-day account work uses a few commands. `usermod -aG docker ana` adds Ana to a supplementary group; without `-a` the `-G` option replaces all her groups, a common mistake that removes access. `passwd -l ana` locks the password, `chage -l ana` shows password ageing, and `userdel -r ana` removes the account and its home directory. `id ana` and `groups ana` show what she belongs to, and changes to groups only apply at her next login.

Edit sudo rules with `visudo`, never directly: it checks the syntax before saving, so a typo cannot lock everyone out of sudo. Prefer dropping files into `/etc/sudoers.d/` and granting specific commands rather than full root, for example `%webops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx`. Review `/var/log/auth.log` or `journalctl _COMM=sudo` to see who used sudo and for what.

lx-text.heading: A worked pipeline: top talkers in a web log
body: Suppose you need the ten IP addresses that made the most requests to a web server. Each line of an nginx or Apache access log starts with the client IP, so `awk '{print $1}' access.log` extracts it. `sort` groups identical addresses together, `uniq -c` counts each group, `sort -rn` orders by count, highest first, and `head -10` keeps the top ten. Joined with pipes: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10`.

The same pattern answers many questions by changing the first step. `grep ' 404 ' access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` lists the most requested missing pages. For anything larger or repeated, `awk` alone can count with an associative array, and `sed -n '/10:00/,/10:05/p'` extracts a time window. Build pipelines one stage at a time and check the output at each step.

lx-packages.heading: Repositories, signing keys and pinning
body: Packages come from repositories listed in `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/` on Debian and Ubuntu, or `/etc/yum.repos.d/` on RHEL and Fedora. Each repository signs its metadata, and the package manager refuses unsigned or wrongly signed packages; that check is what stops a tampered mirror from installing malware. Add third-party repositories only from vendors you trust, with their signing key stored in `/etc/apt/keyrings/` and referenced by `signed-by`, rather than trusting the key for every repository.

On servers, control when packages change. `apt-mark hold nginx` or `dnf versionlock` keeps a package at its current version until you are ready to test an upgrade. Unattended security updates (`unattended-upgrades` or `dnf-automatic`) are a good default for security patches, while larger upgrades go through a test environment first. Universal formats such as Snap and Flatpak bundle their own dependencies and update separately from the system package manager.

lx-systemd.heading: Writing your own service unit
body: To run an application as a managed service, create a unit file such as `/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service`. The `[Unit]` section holds a description and ordering (`After=network-online.target`); `[Service]` sets `ExecStart=/opt/myapp/bin/server`, `User=myapp`, and `Restart=on-failure`; `[Install]` sets `WantedBy=multi-user.target` so `systemctl enable` starts it at boot. Run `systemctl daemon-reload` after creating or editing a unit.

systemd can also sandbox the service with a few lines: `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes` and `ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapp`. `systemd-analyze security myapp` scores how exposed a unit is and lists the options that would tighten it. Override a packaged unit with `systemctl edit nginx`, which writes a drop-in file instead of changing the vendor's original.

lx-network.heading: Troubleshooting a connection step by step
body: When a service cannot be reached, check each layer in turn. `ip addr` and `ip route` confirm the host has an address and a default route. `ping` to the gateway tests the local network, and `ping 1.1.1.1` tests the path out. `dig example.com` (or `resolvectl query`) tests name resolution separately from connectivity. If names fail but IP addresses work, the fault is DNS.

Then test the port itself. On the server, `ss -tlnp` shows whether the service is listening and on which address; a service bound to 127.0.0.1 cannot be reached from other machines. From the client, `nc -zv server 443` or `curl -v https://server` tests the TCP connection and shows TLS errors. If the service listens but the client cannot connect, check the host firewall (`ufw status`, `nft list ruleset`) and any network firewall between them. `tcpdump -i eth0 port 443` shows whether packets arrive at all.

lx-bash.heading: Inputs, quoting and checking your scripts
body: Most broken scripts fail on quoting. Always quote variables, `"$file"` rather than `$file`, so names containing spaces or wildcards are passed as one argument. Use `"$@"` to pass all of a script's arguments on unchanged. Read input with `read -r name`, and check required arguments early: `[[ $# -eq 1 ]] || { echo "usage: $0 <dir>" >&2; exit 2; }`.

Clean up after yourself with a trap: `tmp=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT` deletes the temporary file however the script ends. Before running a script on a server, check it with ShellCheck (`shellcheck deploy.sh`), which catches unquoted variables, unused variables and common logic errors. Running with `bash -x script.sh` prints each command as it executes, which is the fastest way to see where a script goes wrong.

lx-logs.heading: Searching logs effectively
body: journalctl filters are the quickest way to narrow down an event: `journalctl -u nginx --since '2026-05-12 09:00' --until '09:30'` shows one service in a time window, `-p warning` shows warnings and worse, `-b -1` shows the previous boot (useful after a crash), and `-o json-pretty` exposes every field. For classic text logs, `grep -i error /var/log/syslog | tail -50` and `zgrep` for rotated, compressed files cover most needs.

Logs are only useful if they are kept and protected. logrotate compresses and deletes old files on a schedule; check `/etc/logrotate.d/` so logs do not fill the disk. journald keeps logs in memory only unless `/var/log/journal` exists or `Storage=persistent` is set. For security, forward logs to a central server or SIEM, so an attacker who gains root on the host cannot quietly delete the evidence.

lx-secure.heading: Watching for intrusion
body: Hardening reduces the chance of a break-in; monitoring tells you when one happens. Check `/var/log/auth.log` (or `journalctl -u ssh`) for repeated failed logins and successful logins from unexpected addresses. Fail2ban reads those logs and temporarily blocks addresses that fail too often. The `last` and `lastb` commands list recent successful and failed logins.

For deeper visibility, auditd records security-relevant events such as changes to `/etc/passwd` or use of privileged commands, according to rules you define. File integrity monitoring tools such as AIDE record hashes of system files and report changes. Combine them with mandatory access control (SELinux on RHEL-family systems, AppArmor on Ubuntu), left in enforcing mode rather than disabled, so a compromised service is confined to what its policy allows.

tf-variables.heading: Handling secrets and sensitive values
body: Marking a variable or output `sensitive = true` hides it from plan and apply output, but Terraform still writes the value to the state file in plain text. Treat state as sensitive: store it in an encrypted remote backend with tight access, and never commit `terraform.tfstate` or `.tfvars` files that contain secrets to version control.

Better still, keep secrets out of variables. Read them at apply time from a secret manager with a data source (for example `aws_secretsmanager_secret_version`), or let the service generate and manage them; many AWS resources can create and rotate a database password in Secrets Manager for you. Terraform 1.10 added ephemeral values and resources, which are used during a run but never stored in plan or state, and 1.11 added write-only arguments for the same purpose.

tf-expressions.heading: Dynamic blocks and testing expressions
body: Some resources contain repeated nested blocks, such as the ingress rules of a security group. A `dynamic` block generates them from a collection: `dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.ports  content { from_port = ingress.value  to_port = ingress.value  protocol = "tcp"  cidr_blocks = ["10.0.0.0/8"] } }`. Use it sparingly: a few explicit blocks are easier to read than a clever loop.

When an expression gets complicated, test it before using it in a resource. `terraform console` opens an interactive prompt where you can evaluate functions and variables against your configuration, for example `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 2)` returns `10.0.2.0/24`. Functions such as `try()` and `can()` handle optional values, and `lookup(map, key, default)` reads a map with a fallback.

tf-state-backends.heading: Moving and importing resources safely
body: Refactoring code changes resource addresses, and Terraform would otherwise destroy the old address and create a new one. A `moved` block tells it the resource was renamed: `moved { from = aws_instance.web  to = aws_instance.app }`. The plan then shows a move, not a replacement. Moved blocks are reviewable in pull requests, which makes them safer than running `terraform state mv` by hand.

To bring existing infrastructure under Terraform, use an `import` block with the resource address and its ID, then run `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` to produce starting configuration. Review and clean the generated code before applying. To stop managing a resource without deleting it, use a `removed` block (Terraform 1.7+) or `terraform state rm`. Take a state backup, and make sure versioning is on for the backend bucket, before any manual state change.

tf-modules.heading: Testing and publishing modules
body: A module used by many teams needs tests. `terraform validate` catches syntax and type errors; `terraform test` (Terraform 1.6+) runs `.tftest.hcl` files that plan or apply the module with test inputs and check assertions about the result, such as the bucket having encryption enabled. Variable `validation` blocks and `precondition` and `postcondition` checks inside resources give users clear errors at plan time.

Publish modules with a version for every change, following semantic versioning: patch for fixes, minor for backward-compatible additions, major for breaking changes. Include a README with inputs, outputs and an example, and a `versions.tf` that declares the required Terraform and provider versions. Callers then pin a range such as `~> 2.3` and upgrade deliberately.

cpp-basics.heading: Building real projects with CMake
body: Calling the compiler by hand works for one file. Real projects use a build system, and CMake is the de facto standard for C++. A minimal `CMakeLists.txt` declares `cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)`, `project(hello CXX)`, `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)` and `add_executable(hello main.cpp)`. Then `cmake -S . -B build` configures the project and `cmake --build build` compiles it, using whichever compiler and generator the platform provides.

Build in two configurations. A Debug build (`-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`) keeps symbols and turns off optimisation so a debugger can step through code. A Release build turns on optimisation for speed. Add warnings to every build, for example `target_compile_options(hello PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)` with GCC and Clang, and treat new warnings as bugs.

cpp-types.heading: Initialisation and conversions
body: C++ has several ways to initialise a variable, and brace initialisation is the safest default: `int count{0};` or `double rate{0.05};`. Braces refuse narrowing conversions, so `int n{3.7};` is a compile error rather than a silent truncation to 3. An uninitialised local such as `int total;` holds an indeterminate value, and reading it is undefined behaviour, so always initialise.

Mixing signed and unsigned types causes surprising results: `-1 < 1u` is false, because `-1` converts to a huge unsigned value. Compare sizes with `std::ssize()` or cast deliberately, and turn on `-Wsign-compare`. Use `static_cast<int>(x)` when you mean a conversion so it is visible in review; avoid C-style casts such as `(int)x`, which can silently perform more dangerous conversions.

cpp-control-functions.heading: Overloading, default arguments and returning results
body: Functions can share a name if their parameter lists differ: `int area(int side)` and `double area(double w, double h)` are overloads, and the compiler picks one from the argument types. Default arguments supply values the caller may omit: `void log(const std::string& msg, int level = 1);`. Keep defaults in the declaration in the header, not repeated in the definition.

Return results by value: modern compilers elide the copy, and moves make it cheap even when they cannot. To return several values, return a struct or use structured bindings with `std::pair` or `std::tuple`: `auto [min, max] = std::minmax(a, b);`. For a value that may be missing, return `std::optional<T>` rather than a magic number such as -1, so the caller has to check.

cpp-pointers.heading: Choosing between references, pointers and smart pointers
body: Use a reference when the object must exist and you only need to use it: `void print(const Order& o)`. Use a raw pointer when 'nothing' is a valid value and the function does not own the object: `Node* find(int key)` returns `nullptr` when the key is missing. Never use a raw pointer to own memory in modern code; that is the job of `std::unique_ptr` or `std::shared_ptr`.

For a view of a contiguous range, `std::span<int>` (C++20) carries a pointer and a length together, so the function knows the size and cannot be handed a mismatched one. Similarly `std::string_view` views characters without copying. Views must not outlive the data they point to, which is the same dangling risk as a raw pointer.

cpp-oop.heading: The rule of zero, three and five
body: If a class manages a resource directly, such as raw memory or a file handle, it needs a destructor, and then almost certainly a copy constructor and copy assignment operator too (the rule of three), plus a move constructor and move assignment for efficiency (the rule of five). Getting any of these wrong causes double frees or leaks.

The better design is the rule of zero: hold resources in members that already manage themselves, such as `std::vector`, `std::string` and `std::unique_ptr`, and write none of the five. The compiler-generated versions then do the right thing. Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` to stop accidental conversions, and mark overriding functions `override` and classes not meant for inheritance `final`.

cpp-stl.heading: Choosing a container and watching iterator invalidation
body: Start with `std::vector`: its elements sit in contiguous memory, which makes iteration fast and cache-friendly. Use `std::unordered_map` for average constant-time lookups by key, `std::map` when you need keys in sorted order, `std::deque` for cheap insertion at both ends, and `std::array` for a fixed size known at compile time. `std::list` is rarely the best choice despite its cheap middle insertion.

Modifying a container can invalidate iterators, pointers and references into it. A `push_back` that grows a vector reallocates its storage, so any pointer to an element becomes dangling. Erasing inside a loop must use the iterator that `erase` returns: `it = v.erase(it);`. Calling `reserve()` when you know the final size avoids repeated reallocations.

cpp-raii.heading: Exception safety and custom deleters
body: RAII is what makes code exception-safe. If a function acquires two resources by hand and the second acquisition throws, the first leaks unless every path cleans it up. With each resource owned by an object, stack unwinding runs the destructors automatically. Aim for the strong guarantee where it matters: an operation either succeeds completely or leaves the object unchanged, often by doing the work on a copy and swapping it in.

Smart pointers can manage resources other than memory through custom deleters: `std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> f(fopen("log.txt", "r"), &fclose);` closes the file when `f` goes out of scope. Create shared objects with `std::make_shared` and unique ones with `std::make_unique`, and break `shared_ptr` reference cycles with `std::weak_ptr`.

cpp-modern-templates.heading: Ranges and compile-time programming
body: C++20 ranges let you compose operations without writing loops or managing iterator pairs: `for (int x : v | std::views::filter([](int n) { return n % 2 == 0; }) | std::views::transform([](int n) { return n * n; }))` visits the squares of the even numbers lazily, without creating intermediate containers. Algorithms in `std::ranges` take the whole container: `std::ranges::sort(v);`.

Work can move from run time to compile time. A `constexpr` function can be evaluated by the compiler when its arguments are constants, and `consteval` (C++20) requires it. `if constexpr` chooses a branch at compile time inside templates, discarding the other. Combined with concepts, these replace most of the template tricks older C++ code relied on.

cpp-safety.heading: Writing safer C++ day to day
body: Many memory-safety bugs disappear with a few habits. Prefer containers and views (`std::vector`, `std::array`, `std::span`, `std::string_view`) over raw arrays and pointer arithmetic; use `.at()` where an out-of-range index is possible; own memory only through smart pointers; and initialise every variable. The C++ Core Guidelines collect these rules, and clang-tidy checks many of them automatically.

Treat compiler and tool output as part of the build. Enable warnings and make them errors in CI, run tests under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, fuzz code that parses untrusted input, and add static analysis. Hardening options such as `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3`, stack protectors and the standard library's hardened mode catch some remaining errors at run time.

go-structs-interfaces.heading: Designing with small interfaces
body: Go interfaces work best when they are small and defined by the code that uses them. The standard library's `io.Reader` has a single method, `Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)`, yet files, network connections, buffers and HTTP bodies all satisfy it, so one function can read from any of them. Define an interface in the consuming package with only the methods it needs; this keeps dependencies loose and makes testing with a fake easy.

Remember the method-set rule: a method with a pointer receiver belongs to `*T`, not `T`, so a value of type `T` does not satisfy an interface that needs it. Also, an interface holding a typed nil pointer is not itself nil: returning `var p *MyErr = nil` as an `error` gives a non-nil error. Return a literal `nil` when there is no error.

rust-control-functions.heading: Patterns beyond match
body: When you only care about one case, `if let` is shorter than a full `match`: `if let Some(user) = find_user(id) { greet(&user); }`. `let ... else` binds a value or leaves the function early: `let Some(user) = find_user(id) else { return Err(NotFound); };`. `while let` loops as long as a pattern keeps matching, for example popping items from a stack.

Patterns can also destructure tuples and structs and add guards: `match point { (0, y) => ..., (x, 0) => ..., (x, y) if x == y => ..., _ => ... }`. Loops can carry labels so `break 'outer;` exits a nested loop. Because `match` must be exhaustive, the compiler tells you every place to update when you add an enum variant.

rust-ownership.heading: Lifetimes in practice
body: Every reference has a lifetime, the span during which it is valid, and most of the time the compiler infers it. You write lifetime annotations only when a function returns a reference and the compiler cannot tell which input it borrows from: `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` says the result lives no longer than both inputs. Annotations describe relationships; they never extend how long data lives.

When the borrow checker refuses code, the fix is usually structural rather than a battle with annotations. Return owned data (`String` instead of `&str`) when the caller should keep it, clone a small value when sharing is awkward, shorten a borrow by ending it before the mutation, or restructure so one function owns the data. For genuinely shared ownership, `Rc<T>` (single thread) or `Arc<T>` (across threads) count references at run time.

rust-structs-enums.heading: Traits: shared behaviour
body: Traits define behaviour that several types can implement, similar to interfaces. `trait Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64; }` is implemented with `impl Shape for Circle { ... }`. Generic functions accept any implementor: `fn total<T: Shape>(shapes: &[T]) -> f64`, and the compiler generates a specialised copy for each type. When you need a mix of types in one collection, use a trait object: `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`, which dispatches at run time.

Many common traits can be derived instead of written: `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` gives printing, copying and comparison. Implementing standard traits such as `Display`, `From` and `Default` makes your types work naturally with the rest of the language, for example letting `?` convert errors automatically through `From`.

rust-errors.heading: Designing error types
body: Libraries should return errors that callers can inspect. Define an enum with one variant per failure, implement `std::error::Error` and `Display`, and implement `From` for the underlying errors so `?` converts them. The `thiserror` crate generates this boilerplate from attributes. Applications that mainly report errors can use `anyhow`, which wraps any error and lets you add context: `.context("reading config file")?`.

Reserve `panic!`, `unwrap()` and `expect()` for bugs, not expected failures. A missing file or bad user input is an error to return; an index that should be impossible is a bug. In tests and prototypes `expect("why this cannot fail")` is acceptable and documents the assumption; in production code paths, propagate with `?` or handle the error explicitly.
